name: THE MR. SMITH GOES TO SQUASH-INGTON BURGER

recipe.history:
Winter squash — the genus Cucurbita — has a history in the Americas that predates European contact by thousands of years. Squash is one of the 'Three Sisters' of Indigenous North American agriculture, cultivated alongside corn and beans in a mutually beneficial polyculture system developed by numerous Indigenous peoples across the continent. Archaeological evidence of squash cultivation in Mexico dates back over ten thousand years, making it one of the earliest domesticated plants in the Western Hemisphere. Butternut squash (Cucurbita moschata), with its characteristic tan skin and sweet, dense orange flesh, was developed in the Americas and did not reach Europe until after Columbus's first voyage in 1492. Acorn squash (Cucurbita pepo), with its distinctive ridged, dark green exterior and nutty, yellow-orange flesh, was similarly a New World crop, named for its acorn-like shape. The Pilgrims and early European settlers in North America learned to cultivate and cook squash from Indigenous peoples, and it quickly became a foundational crop of colonial American agriculture. Butternut squash's rich sweetness made it ideal for soups and purees; acorn squash's denser texture suited it for roasting whole or in halves, stuffed with butter and brown sugar. Both varieties have been part of the American harvest table since the 17th century, and both appear in this burger as a puree and as crisped chips, honoring their full textural and flavor range.

Squash entered the American culinary mainstream in multiple forms and waves. Pumpkin pie, made from a closely related species, became a Thanksgiving tradition in the 17th century and helped cement the cultural association between squash and American autumn. By the 20th century, butternut squash soup had become a restaurant classic, its velvety texture and natural sweetness easy to love and endlessly adaptable with spice, cream, or vinegar. The farm-to-table movement of the late 20th century elevated squash from humble harvest vegetable to something more serious: butternut squash risotto, acorn squash roasted with miso, delicata squash rings fried in brown butter. The craft burger world latched onto squash as a topping because it solves a specific problem — how to add natural sweetness, earthiness, and textural interest to a burger without resorting to sugar or processed condiments. A properly made butternut squash purée, seasoned with brown butter, nutmeg, and a touch of maple, is sweet, rich, and faintly savory all at once — a perfect foil for the salted, umami-rich depth of a beef patty. Acorn squash chips, sliced thin and fried or roasted until they shatter, add crunch and visual drama.

Squash and I have a seasonal relationship: each autumn, when the markets fill up with their sprawling, colorful displays of winter squash in every shape and size, I feel something close to happiness. There is a particular pleasure in cutting open a butternut squash — the slight resistance of the skin giving way to the dense, fragrant flesh, the color a deep burnt orange — and knowing that you are about to make something that will smell like autumn cooking itself. I make butternut squash purée every October without fail, usually cooking more than I need because the surplus keeps well in the refrigerator and improves over a day or two as the flavors deepen. I have put it on pasta, stirred it into polenta, used it as a pizza sauce, and eaten it cold from the refrigerator with a spoon. Putting it on a burger — the idea arriving one evening when I had a batch in the refrigerator and a patty in the pan — felt immediately, perfectly right. The sweetness and the salt, the soft and the crispy, the orange and the brown. This burger is autumn on a bun.

The butternut squash purée on this burger is soft, sweet, and gentle, which makes the cooking temperature of the patty especially important. A medium rare patty — 130–135°F — has a juicy, meaty interior that provides a textural and flavor counterpoint to the silky purée; the purée's sweetness is balanced by the savory richness of the beef fat. Cook the patty to well-done and you eliminate that counterpoint: the dry, compact beef melds with the purée rather than contrasting it, and what should be a layered, complex bite becomes a uniform sweetness. The acorn squash chips add the crunch that the well-done patty can no longer provide, but they cannot replace the yielding, juicy center of a properly cooked medium rare patty. Medium rare is what gives this burger its structure: the layering of textures and temperatures that makes each bite interesting.
ingredients: 1 medium butternut squash (about 2 lbs), halved and seeds removed
2–4 tbsp warm cream or stock (to thin to spreading consistency)
For the sage and hazelnut gremolata:
¼ cup hazelnuts, toasted, skins removed, roughly chopped
2 tbsp fresh sage, very finely sliced (chiffonade)
4 honey wheat buns, split and toasted
instructions: 1. Make honey wheat buns: Dissolve yeast in warm water with honey. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine both flours and salt. Add yeast mixture, butter, and egg. Knead on medium 8–10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Place in oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1–1½ hours until doubled.

2. Divide dough into 6 balls, place on parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and press pumpkin seeds on top. Bake 18–20 minutes until golden. Cool completely.

3. Make the acorn squash chips: Preheat oven to 400°F. Using a very sharp knife or mandoline, slice the acorn squash (unpeeled) crosswise into rounds ⅛-inch thick. Remove and discard any seeds from the center rings. Toss slices with olive oil, salt, pepper, smoked paprika, and cayenne. Spread on parchment-lined baking sheets in a single layer. Bake 18–22 minutes, flipping once halfway, until golden brown and beginning to crisp. Watch closely — they can burn quickly. Transfer to a wire rack; they will crisp further as they cool. Work in batches if necessary.

4. Make brown butter: Melt butter in a small light-colored saucepan over medium heat. Cook, swirling frequently, until the foam subsides and the milk solids turn deep golden brown and smell nutty, about 4–5 minutes. Pour immediately into a bowl to stop cooking. Reserve 2 tbsp for the squash purée.

5. Make the butternut squash purée: Roast squash halves cut-side down on a baking sheet at 400°F for 40–50 minutes until completely tender and caramelized on the cut face. Scoop flesh into a food processor or blender. Add 2 tbsp regular butter, 2 tbsp brown butter, nutmeg, maple syrup, salt, and white pepper. Process until completely smooth. Add warm cream or stock a tablespoon at a time until the purée reaches a thick but spreadable consistency. Taste and adjust salt and sweetness.
6. Make the sage and hazelnut gremolata: Combine chopped hazelnuts, sliced sage, lemon zest, olive oil, and salt in a small bowl. Toss and set aside.

7. Form patties: Gently combine ground beef with salt, pepper, garlic powder, smoked paprika, and cinnamon. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into ¾-inch-thick patties with a center dimple.

8. Cook patties: Heat a cast iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side. Flip. Add butter to the pan and baste patties for 1–2 minutes. Add white cheddar to each patty and cover briefly to melt. Remove when internal temperature reads 130–135°F for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
9. Toast buns: Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat and toast buns cut-side down 2–3 minutes until golden.

10. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of butternut squash purée on the bottom bun. Place the medium rare patty with melted cheddar on top of the purée. Add a small handful of baby arugula. Stack 4–5 acorn squash chips over the arugula, angling them for visual height. Scatter a spoonful of sage and hazelnut gremolata over the top. Drizzle with a thin thread of maple syrup if desired. Finish with flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun (spread the inside with a thin layer of squash purée as well). Serve immediately.
